title: V'Zot HaBerachah: no one knows his grave (Deuteronomy 34:5–6)
hook: God buries Moses, and no one knows his grave to this day

segments.voice: Yesterday, the view from Nebo. Your line was see it from the mountain. What goal did you look at? Today, the death of Moses, and a strange detail about his grave. Day five hundred thirty-five.

Great people usually get great graves. Pyramids. Mausoleums. Marble statues in town squares. Pilgrims travel thousands of miles to stand where famous bodies lie, and the resting place of a founder can become a shrine almost overnight. People leave flowers, candles, notes, stones. Some graves draw crowds for centuries. The Torah's greatest teacher dies on a mountain in Moab. And the text goes out of its way to tell us there is nothing to visit.
screen: `PYRAMIDS AND MAUSOLEUMS.` → `PILGRIMS AT THE TOMB.` → `NOTHING TO VISIT.`

segments.voice: So Moses, the servant of God, dies there in the land of Moab, at God's word. He is buried in a valley opposite Beth-peor, the text says, "and no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day." Who buried him? The Hebrew simply says: he buried him. Rashi says it was God, in His glory. The Talmud, in Sotah, takes that seriously and turns it into a teaching about how people should live. God clothed Adam and Eve. God visited Abraham when he was healing. God comforted Isaac when he mourned. And God buried Moses. So, the Talmud says, walk in God's ways: clothe, visit, comfort, bury. When volunteers of a chevra kadisha, a Jewish burial society, care for the body of someone who has died, they're walking in that line. And the hidden grave? The text doesn't say why. A common explanation is that the people would have made it a place of worship, and Moses had always pointed beyond himself. Whatever the reason, the effect is clear. No shrine. No relic. What remains of Moses is what he taught. And the teaching isn't left in one place. It's in every Torah scroll, in every synagogue, read aloud week by week. Moses' grave is unknown. His words are everywhere.
screen: `MOSES DIES IN THE LAND OF MOAB.` · `WHO BURIED HIM?` · `CLOTHE, VISIT, COMFORT, BURY.` · `NO SHRINE, ONLY TEACHING.` · then, large: `NO GRAVE, ONLY TEACHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let a legacy be the teaching. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who has died whose words or habits still live in you. A grandmother's saying, a teacher's correction, a friend's way of laughing at trouble. You don't need a grave to find them. Where do they show up in your own life? Name one thing they taught you. Then think of one thing you'd like to pass on in the same way, so that it outlasts you. The bell holds the time.
V'Zot HaBerachah. And this is the blessing. A portion that ends with a death, an unknown grave, and a teaching that stays.
Your line: no grave, only teaching. Today, pass on one thing someone taught you, and say their name when you do. Day five hundred thirty-five.

howItsDone: Caring for the dead is considered one of the highest acts of kindness in Jewish life; local chevra kadisha societies prepare bodies for burial, and the anniversary of Moses' death is traditionally kept on the 7th of Adar, a day some burial societies mark.

notes: Deuteronomy 34:6 final clause quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; verify. The rest of 34:5–6 is paraphrased.
Rashi on 34:6: 'He buried him: the Holy One, blessed be He, in His glory'. Paraphrased.
Sotah 14a: clothe the naked (Adam and Eve), visit the sick (Abraham), comfort mourners (Isaac), bury the dead (Moses). Paraphrased.
'So the grave would not become a place of worship' is a common explanation, not stated in the text; kept as 'a common explanation'.
7 Adar as Moses' yahrzeit (Megillah 13b) is mentioned only in howItsDone; verify the chevra kadisha custom.
